summary: A 1980 specification of the Telnet protocol, which gives remote text terminal access across the network. It was replaced by RFC 854.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 764 describes Telnet, which lets a terminal communicate with a remote computer using shared rules for text and control commands. It uses a common virtual terminal model and lets both ends agree on optional features; RFC 854 later replaced this specification.

questions: what is a network virtual terminal
subtitle: An early Telnet specification for exchanging terminal data and control commands over TCP.

tldr.problem: Different computers and terminals needed a common way to exchange terminal data without requiring each host to know the other's local device details.
tldr.mechanism: Telnet carries data and control commands over TCP, maps each end to a Network Virtual Terminal, and lets peers negotiate optional features.
tldr.outcome: This Telnet specification was obsoleted by RFC 854.

today: RFC 764 was obsoleted by RFC 854, the later Telnet specification.

sections.title: A Shared Terminal Protocol
sections.content:
Telnet provides a two-way, byte-oriented communications facility intended to connect terminal devices with terminal-oriented processes. A Telnet connection is a TCP connection that carries ordinary data with Telnet control information mixed into the stream.

The protocol relies on a Network Virtual Terminal (NVT), negotiated options, and a symmetric view of the two endpoints. Each host maps its local terminal and conventions to the shared NVT model.
sections.plainLanguage: Telnet gives both computers shared rules for sending terminal text and commands. Each computer translates between those rules and its own local terminal.

sections.title: Negotiating Optional Features
sections.content:
Either endpoint can request an option, and the other can accept or reject it. WILL offers to perform an option; DO asks the other endpoint to perform it. WON'T and DON'T reject or stop options. When an option is rejected, the connection stays with the NVT behavior.

Endpoints should request only changes of state and should not acknowledge a request to enter a mode they already use. They should not repeat a rejected request until something changes. These rules prevent the symmetric exchanges from becoming endless loops.
sections.plainLanguage: Each side can ask to use an extra feature, and the other side can accept or refuse. They ask only when the setting needs to change, which prevents repeated replies from looping.

sections.title: The Network Virtual Terminal
sections.content:
The NVT is an imaginary two-way device with a keyboard and printer. Its character set is seven-bit USASCII in an eight-bit field. By default, it is treated as half-duplex and line-buffered. When a process has finished sending and needs input before it can continue, it sends the Go Ahead command.

The NVT uses CR LF for a new line and CR NUL for a carriage return alone. It also defines standard representations for functions such as Interrupt Process, Abort Output, Are You There, Erase Character, and Erase Line.
sections.plainLanguage: The NVT is a shared model of a keyboard and printer, including rules for characters and line endings. Each computer translates that model into the behavior of its real terminal.

sections.title: Commands and Connection Port
sections.content:
A Telnet command starts with the IAC escape character and a command code. Option-negotiation commands use a third byte to identify the option. To send the IAC byte as ordinary data, it is doubled. The RFC assigns command codes for functions including Data Mark, Interrupt Process, Go Ahead, and the option-negotiation verbs.

For remote terminal access, the server listens on TCP port 23.
sections.plainLanguage: A command begins with a special escape byte, followed by a code that tells the receiver what to do. For remote terminal access, the server listens on TCP port 23.
